title: Lysosomes in Pathology
subject: Pathology
summary: Lysosomes are acidic organelles packed with hydrolases that digest intracellular material and extracellular debris. In disease they can accumulate, leak, or be deficient, leading to cellular dysfunction and clinical syndromes.

sections.p: Lysosomes are membrane‑bound organelles containing acid hydrolases (proteases, lipases, nucleases). They fuse with endosomes, phagosomes and autophagosomes to degrade cargo. Diagnosis is usually indirect, via histology or functional assays.

t.b: Assesses specific lysosomal hydrolase function; low activity indicates a storage disorder
Visualises characteristic inclusions (e.g., zebra bodies in Fabry disease)

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and functional impairment. For storage disorders, the International Consensus Staging System (ICSS) uses biomarkers and clinical features.

t.b: Measures lysosomal enzyme levels and substrate accumulation; guides prognosis

sections.p: Causes include inherited enzyme deficiencies, secondary accumulation from infections, or drug‑induced lysosomal dysfunction. In low‑resource settings, infections such as HIV, TB, malaria, and schistosomiasis can overwhelm lysosomal capacity.

sections.p: Clinical features depend on the organ system. Common presentations include hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, renal dysfunction, and neurological deficits. Infections may present with fever, rash, or organ failure.

t.b: Look for organomegaly, skin changes, and neurological signs

sections.p: Investigations are tailored to the suspected cause and available resources. In low‑resource settings, basic labs and imaging are prioritized.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid organ failure, unexplained fever, or neurological decline. Complications can be fatal if not addressed promptly.

faq.q: What is the main function of lysosomes?
faq.a: They digest intracellular and extracellular material via acid hydrolases.
They increase the load of debris and can overwhelm lysosomal capacity, leading to cellular dysfunction.

faq.q: Why is enzyme replacement therapy limited in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: High cost and need for cold storage make ERT challenging where resources are scarce.

exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV patient develops hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias. What is the most likely mechanism? — Excessive macrophage activation leading to lysosomal overload and hemophagocytosis.
A child presents with bone pain and renal tubular acidosis. Which lysosomal storage disorder is most likely? — Fabry disease; look for angiokeratomas and neuropathic pain.
During a malaria outbreak, a patient develops acute kidney injury. Which drug should be avoided to prevent further lysosomal damage? — Chloroquine; it accumulates in lysosomes and can cause toxicity.
A patient with Gaucher disease is started on ERT. What is the main benefit? — Reduction of glucocerebroside accumulation, improving organomegaly and cytopenias.
A 45‑year‑old woman with unexplained jaundice has normal LFTs but enlarged spleen. What investigation should you order? — Ultrasound to assess splenic size and look for storage inclusions.
A patient with suspected lysosomal storage disease has normal enzyme assay results. What could explain this? — Sample degradation during transport or assay interference; repeat with proper handling.
In a low‑resource setting, how would you monitor a patient on hydroxychloroquine for lysosomal toxicity? — Periodic visual acuity and fundus examination.
A patient with a lysosomal storage disorder develops seizures. What is the most likely cause? — CNS involvement due to substrate accumulation in neurons.
